newsitem.title: UK: BA looking at alternatives to American deal.
newsitem.headline: BA looking at alternatives to American deal.

text.p: British Airways Plc said on Monday it was still hopeful it could win approval for its proposed alliance with American Airlines but has contingency plans in place should the deal be blocked by the European or U.S. regulatory authorities.

BA has already threatened to abandon the deal if regulatory approvals are not granted before November, having struggled for more than a year to agree terms with the European and U.S. competition authorities.

"There are always fallback alternatives and obviously we have our contingency plans but a deal with American would certainly be the most attractive in the commercial sense, depending on the regulatory price," finance director Derek Stevens told Reuters on Monday.
He was speaking after the airline reported first-quarter results.
"If the regulators are going to make it too expensive to do then of course we have to look at alternatives," he said. "There has to be a time limit on this," he added.
BA said in its results statement on Monday it was continuing discussions with the authorities on both sides of the Atlantic but the process was progressing "very slowly".
"British Airways is continuing to have discussions with the Office of Fair Trading in London, the Competition Directorate in Brussels and the Department of Justice in Washington.

"The airline has provided all of these bodies and the (U.S.) Department of Transportation with the information and documents that they have requested, which hopefully will enable them to reach a conclusion in the next few months," BA said.
Under the proposed alliance, BA intends to co-ordinate its 244 flights a week to 22 U.S. destinations with American's 238 flights from seven U.S. airports to 12 European destinations.

But rival airlines, the European Union's Competition Commissioner and consumer groups have all objected to the deal, alleging that it would dominate Europe's biggest trans-Atlantic market and lead to higher fares.

BA and American argue that the deal would lead to lower fares because it would only go ahead if Britain and the U.S. agree a new open skies aviation trade pact to open up the market to free competition.

They also argue that they must be allowed to compete against rival transatlantic alliances which already have approvals for important transfer traffic in what they say is becoming an increasingly global market.

Britain's Office of Fair Trading (OFT) proposed last December that BA and American should release 168 weekly runway slots at Heathrow -- enough to operate 12 daily return flights -- to give other airlines room to compete.

But industry sources say The European Union's Competition Commissioner has suggested to BA and the OFT that it should release 350 weekly slots at Heathrow, which is a far higher number than BA would ever be willing to give up.
"Obviously there have been discussions going on...but that's not to say that BA remotely would see that sort of deal making sense," said one source on Monday.
